title: Coiling technique (rush and seagrass)
subtitle: How to start, build, and finish a coiled basket in rush or seagrass rope
excerpt: Coiling is the structural technique behind seagrass and rush baskets: a thick rope core is spiralled outward and upward while a thin binding thread stitches each new coil to the one beneath. This guide covers the two critical transitions where most first attempts fail: starting the coil and finishing the rim.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the coiling construction method; Cassell's Book of the Household (1890) for the rush and seagrass variants.

glossaryTerms.definition: Basket construction where a thick rope core coils in a spiral and is stitched to each adjacent coil with a binding thread.
Twisted rope from dried marine grass. Available from craft suppliers. Stiff enough to coil without soaking.
Dried stems of bulrush or soft rush. Must be dampened before working to prevent snapping.
Flat natural strips from the raffia palm, used as the binding thread to stitch coils together.

content.text: The coiling technique is one of the oldest basketry methods: the same structural principle appears in baskets from ancient Egypt and in contemporary seagrass fruit bowls. The technique has three moving parts, the core rope that forms the structure, the binding thread that stitches the coils together, and the bodkin that creates the path for each stitch. Getting these three in rhythm is the whole skill.
, or sweetgrass. The technique is identical regardless of the core material; what changes is the preparation (seagrass needs no soaking; rush needs dampening; sweetgrass is used dry).
Core material: seagrass rope (6 mm) or bundled rush. Pre-dampen rush in a damp cloth for 1, 2 hours.
Bodkin: blunt-tipped, large eye, for opening stitch holes.

The start is the most critical point, a loose start means the centre of the base will always flex. Two methods work: the fold start (fold the rope tip back 4 cm, bind the fold tightly, then thread the binding through the fold loop to lock) or the knotted start (tie the rope tip into a tight knot, then wrap the binding around the knot several times to secure). The fold start is neater on seagrass rope; the knotted start is easier for rush, which frays at the tip.
Coil the rope tightly around the start and stitch each new coil to the previous one. The stitch: wrap the

raffia three times around the new coil, drive the bodkin through the previous coil, and pull the raffia through and snug. Stitch every 15, 20 mm. The base is complete when it has reached the planned diameter. Keep it flat throughout, set a heavy book on the base whenever you pause.

The transition from flat base to vertical sides is the most common place where first attempts fail. It is made by placing each new coil on top of the outer edge of the previous coil rather than alongside it. The shape of the basket (straight sides, flared sides, or inward-curving sides) is controlled entirely by how far inward or outward each new coil is placed relative to the previous one. Straight sides: each coil placed exactly on top of the outer edge of the previous coil. Flared: each coil placed slightly outward. Inward-curving: each coil placed slightly inward.

Taper the rope end over the last 10 cm by reducing its bulk, for seagrass rope, cut away the outer strands with secateurs; for rush, simply allow the bundle to naturally thin out at the end. Stitch the tapered end snugly against the previous coil, placing stitches every 8 mm to secure it firmly. Thread the final raffia length through the previous coil twice, pull tight, and trim flush.

attrs.symptom: The centre of the base flexes and bends when the basket is pressed
attrs.cause: The start was not locked tightly enough; the fold or knot is slipping
attrs.fix: Reinforce the centre by threading a length of raffia from the outside in through the centre, pulling tight, and knotting on the underside. Do this while the base is still flat and the base material is slightly damp.

attrs.symptom: The sides lean inward rather than staying vertical
attrs.cause: Each new coil is being placed slightly inside the previous coil's outer edge rather than directly on top
attrs.fix: Use a straight-sided form (a round tin or pot of the right diameter) inside the basket as a guide: each new coil should sit just clear of the form's outer edge, not pressed against it.
